rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Before Adam entered the world, God secured his exclusive worship and obedience; the later account of this covenant is in 7:172–173.
rows.anchor: Before sending Adam (sws) in this world, He actually took a promise from him to worship and obey Him only.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: God promised Adam’s descendants messengers; following their guidance brings success, while arrogantly evading it brings destruction.
rows.anchor: God promised the progeny of Adam (sws) that He will send messengers to guide them

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The promised messenger mission continued, and the accounts of those messengers are set out in verses 59–92.
rows.anchor: Then in accordance with this promise, He continued to send messengers. Its details are stated in verses 59-92 ahead.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Past peoples who strayed from monotheism and spread disorder were warned through messengers; rejecting the warnings led to their removal and replacement, testing successors’ use of authority.
rows.anchor: whenever the progeny Adam (sws) spread disorder in the land by deviating from the path of monotheism, they were warned by God through His messengers.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A nation entrusted with authority to repair disorder commits a graver wrong if it creates disorder in what had been set right.
rows.anchor: it did not further disrupt an already disrupted thing; it disrupted what had been set right. This makes its crime to be graver.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Through messengers, truth becomes unmistakable: the system they destroy is evil, and the system they establish is truth.
rows.anchor: Through them, the truth shines like the sun. For this reason, the system which is destroyed by them is evil

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Muhammad is the final messenger, but moral principles governing nations’ rise and fall continue to apply; neither outcome is mere chance.
rows.anchor: Muḥammad (sws) was the last of the messengers but it does not mean that after him the principle of rise and fall of nations has changed.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A nation’s moral elements may explain its survival or dominance, but dominance alone does not establish that the nation or its system is wholly true.
rows.anchor: If a nation is at its zenith, it does show that it has more moral elements that give it life than a vanquished nation.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: National bias attributes another nation’s victory to deceit and misses both its moral strengths and one’s own moral weakness.
rows.anchor: People who are inflicted with national bias always think that the dominance of a victorious nation is because of its deceptive measures and connivances.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: People overawed by a dominant nation treat its dominance as proof of truth and praise its disorder as order; both extremes corrupt national history.
rows.anchor: people who have the mentality of being over-awed think that every dominant nation’s dominance is proof enough of it being on the truth.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: These biases produce badly compiled histories and prevent sound conclusions for collective reform; Islahi says he will elaborate under Sūrah al-Rūm.
rows.anchor: histories of nations were compiled in a totally wrong way. As a result, deriving correct results out of it

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Miscompiled histories make sound lessons for collective reform impossible; Islahi says he will elaborate on this in his explanation of Sūrah al-Rūm.
rows.anchor: for collective reformation became impossible. I will elaborate more on this issue in the explanation of Sūrah al-Rūm

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The call to invoke God humbly and privately describes how to pray; calling on Him alone in fear and hope supplies the motive that removes polytheism.
rows.anchor: The latter depicts the way in which God should be invoked which was opposite to arrogance and the former actually states the motive to invoke God

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Arrogance makes a person indifferent to God; restraining it yields contentment and humility that connect a person to God.
rows.anchor: Arrogance makes a person indifferent to God. If it is controlled, a person becomes content and humble and this links him to God.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Human instincts and external circumstances fall under hope or fear: people desire some things and seek distance from others.
rows.anchor: There are two aspects of this contentment: fear and hope. The instincts of human beings are also divided into these two aspects.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Monotheism requires seeking from God alone what one desires and seeking refuge in Him alone from what one fears or avoids.
rows.anchor: it is the requirement of monotheism that human beings only seek and invoke God. They should turn to Him regarding whatever they desire

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: God alone gives or withholds, protects from evil, and defines good and evil; exclusive reliance helps people decide what to pursue or avoid.
rows.anchor: He alone gives or otherwise. Without Him, none can receive anything good nor remain secure from anything evil. Moreover, He alone is the true standard of good and evil.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Hope and fear are both dangerous openings through which Satan entangles people in overt or hidden polytheism.
rows.anchor: hope and fear can both prove to be dangerous pitfalls. Satan ambushes people through both and thereby entangles them either in open or in hidden polytheism.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Those fully devoted to God as their real Lord and protector in hope and fear are the thorough people near to His mercy.
rows.anchor: people who regard God to be their real Lord and protector in both hope and fear

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Because mercy’s feminine gender is unreal, a feminine pronoun is not required when referring to it.
rows.anchor: it is not essential to use a feminine pronoun while referring to it.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The faʿīl form can serve either masculine or feminine gender in some contexts.
rows.anchor: the fa‘īl form in some situations is equal for the masculine as well as the feminine gender.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Here raḥmah means rain, a Qur’anic usage; the rain parable teaches that only God should be invoked in hope and fear because He alone sends life-giving rain.
rows.anchor: connotes rain here. The Qur’ ān has used this word for rain on more than one occasion.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: God brings monsoon winds that lift water-laden clouds and drive them to barren lands, demonstrating that rain comes only by His command.
rows.anchor: Not a single drop of rain, on which depends life of this whole world, can come down except at God’s behest.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The same image appears in 42:28: God sends rain when people have lost hope and spreads His mercy.
rows.anchor: In verse 28 of S ūrah Shūrā, the words are:

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Aqalla means to lift something as if it had no weight.
rows.anchor: to lift something as if it has no weight.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Saḥāb is the plural of saḥābah though singular in form, which explains the singular pronoun in saqnāhu.
rows.anchor: it is singular in form and shape. For this reason, a singular pronoun is used for it

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The preposition bi in fa-anzalnā bihi marks locus; the signs direct people to God’s power and mercy and to invoking Him alone.
rows.anchor: signifies locus. The verses direct our attention to His power and mercy and as a consequence to ask from Him alone in hope and fear.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: As rain revives dead land, God will raise all the dead; this visible power points to the Hereafter, and the signs aim to remind people of it.
rows.anchor: just as God through rain brings to life a dead stretch of land in a similar way He will bring all the dead back to life.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Ṭayyib and khabīth can describe material as well as moral qualities; here they mean fertile and barren land.
rows.anchor: they also occur in the material sense. Here occasion evidences that the expression

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The omitted parallel in the first half of the sentence means ‘lush’ and ‘more in number,’ while the contrary term means ‘defective’ and ‘little in number.’
rows.anchor: It means “defective” and “little in number.” For this reason, the meaning of “lush” and “more in number

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Rain falls on all surfaces, but its benefit depends on their potential: fertile land flourishes, whereas barren land stays lifeless or grows useless shrubs.
rows.anchor: God’s merciful rain falls on all types of surfaces; however, its benefit is dependent on the potential found in the surface.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Qur’an is mercy like rain, yet only people with intact natural capacities benefit; wasted capacities produce malice and enmity instead of an orchard.
rows.anchor: Only those who have the potential benefit from it. Thus, those whose natural abilities are intact, will become blossom like an orchard.

rows.speaker: Prophet (sws)
rows.claim: The Prophet says he was sent with knowledge and guidance and compares his teaching to rain absorbed by fertile land.
rows.anchor: a narrative of the Prophet (sws). It is reported that he said that he has been sent with knowledge and guidance.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: In the parable’s continuation, receptive people who understand religious teaching benefit others by learning and teaching.
rows.anchor: This is a parable of people who acquire an understanding of religion and benefit from it from what I have been sent with from God.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The continuation also portrays people who do not attend to the teaching as evading its guidance.
rows.anchor: This is also a parable of those who do not direct their attention to it and evade seeking guidance from it.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The rain parable affirms monotheism.
rows.anchor: it lays credence to the belief of monotheism

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The parable offers an analogy for the possibility of the Hereafter and the manifestation of the Day of Judgement.
rows.anchor: a parallel is also furnished of the possibility of the Hereafter and the manifestation of the Day of Judgement

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The parable also makes God’s practice of providing guidance evident.
rows.anchor: the practice of God about providing guidance also becomes evident.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: These parable lessons allude in principle to the topics raised from the beginning of the sūrah through this point.
rows.anchor: all the topics that were raised in this sūrah from its beginning until here are, in principle, alluded to.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Every object in the universe witnesses to the Qur’an’s claims for anyone with a discerning eye, though people lack insightful eyes and ears.
rows.anchor: every object in it bears witness to the facts the Qur’ān is calling them to profess faith in.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The word used for the diverse presentation of verses means ‘to cause to circulate’; it is used for winds elsewhere and here for Qur’anic verses.
rows.anchor: This word is used in the Qur’ ān for winds. It is used here for its verses.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: As winds circulate, God displays diverse signs of power, wisdom, mercy, and retribution; through the Qur’an He likewise makes signs evident in varied ways for recognition and appreciation.
rows.anchor: through the circulation of winds various manifestations of God’s power and wisdom, mercy and retribution come into being

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Explaining facts through varied verses is a divine favor for those who value it; gratitude means properly valuing blessings, on which their benefit depends.
rows.anchor: The essence of gratitude is to duly value favours and blessings. It is on this acknowledgement that the benefit of each blessing is based.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Section VI reinforces warnings of the Hereafter to Quraysh with Arabian nations’ histories: they received political authority, became ungrateful and unjust, rejected messengers and were destroyed after respite. Quraysh face the same situation and impending judgment.
rows.anchor: The purpose of narrating these anecdotes to the Quraysh is that they too are facing the same situation and their fate is about to be decided by God’s court of justice

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: After the covenant reminder, the Israelites’ example warns Quraysh against ingratitude toward God’s favors.
rows.anchor: After they are reminded of the above-mentioned covenant, the example of the Israelites is presented before them.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Israel did not value God’s favor and chose lowliness despite His wish to raise them; warning and favor affect them alike, like a dog whose tongue hangs whether loved or scolded.
rows.anchor: God always wanted to lift them, but they were always inclined to lowliness. Just as how a dog’s tongue dangles from his tongue whether one expresses love for him or scold him

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: People should value their eyes, ears, hearts, and minds and use them rightly instead of blindly following their forefathers’ religion.
rows.anchor: they are asked to value the gifts of eyes, ears, hearts and minds they have and are invited to use them in the right way.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Those who leave their intellectual and sensory faculties unused and keep falling after reminders are consigned to Hell by God.
rows.anchor: people who do not use the abilities of their head and heart and the faculties of their hearing and sight

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Quraysh are directed to the Prophet and told that the bearer of an imminent great danger is neither mad nor possessed.
rows.anchor: the person who is informing them of an imminent great danger is not mad or possessed.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The universe has a wise purpose, so the Prophet’s warned-of decision may be near; his inability to give its exact time does not make it uncertain, since a prophet only brings glad tidings and warnings and does not know the future.
rows.anchor: If he is not able to tell them about its exact time of arrival, it does not mean that it is not certain to come.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: People receive every favor from God yet thank others and associate partners incapable of benefiting or harming them.
rows.anchor: while they receive all favours from God, they thank and appreciate others. They associate such partners with God who can neither benefit nor harm them.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Prophet is urged to remain steadfast against opponents’ baseless objections and is shown what can help him persevere.
rows.anchor: At the end, the Prophet (sws) is urged to be steadfast in the wake of the nonsensical statements of his opponents and their baseless objections.
